If you decide not to sell it, these units are actually a gold mine for someone who likes to tinker with hardware and electronics.

High-Value Parts for Harvesting

Since you mentioned you're into hardware and 3D printing, here is what is actually worth pulling out:

  • The High-Voltage Transformer (MOT): This is the "holy grail" for DIY electronics. You can rewound these to create a high-current, low-voltage power supply for a DIY spot welder (great for battery packs) or use it for Lichtenberg figure wood burning (though please be extremely careful, as MOTs are notoriously lethal).
  • The Turntable Motor: These are usually high-torque, low-RPM AC synchronous motors. They are fantastic for building 3D printing filament drying racks, motorized camera sliders, or even a slow-rotating display stand.
  • Microswitches: There are usually 3 or 4 high-quality Cherry-style microswitches behind the door latch. These are perfect for 3D printer end-stops or custom input buttons for electronics projects.
  • The Magnetron: Inside are two very strong Neodymium ring magnets. If you break down the magnetron (carefully, avoiding the ceramic insulators which can contain beryllium oxide), those magnets are incredibly useful for shop organization or mounting 3D printed parts to metal surfaces.
  • The Cooling Fan: Usually a sturdy shaded-pole motor and fan assembly. It’s great for a DIY soldering fume extractor or cooling a small server rack.

Important Safety Warning

The High-Voltage Capacitor: Even if the microwave has been unplugged for days, the large capacitor inside can hold a lethal charge. If you open this up to harvest parts, your first step must be to safely discharge that capacitor using an insulated screwdriver or a discharge resistor.

If you’re leaning toward selling, listing it for $40–$60 on a local marketplace would likely get it moved quickly. Otherwise, that transformer alone is a fun weekend project waiting to happen.

turns.prompt_text: I've been worried about capacitors with charge for a while but never really knew how to dissipate them correctly. do I have to just touch them with a screwdriver or do I need to ground them into the ground?
turns.response_html:
It’s completely valid to be wary of those capacitors—in a microwave, they can hold around 2,000V to 5,000V, which is more than enough to be lethal.

The "screwdriver trick" is common in hobbyist videos, but doing it raw is actually quite dangerous. It can cause a massive spark, weld the screwdriver tip to the terminal, or even cause the capacitor to fail violently.

Here is the grounded, professional way to handle it:

1. Don't Just "Touch" It

You should never use a bare screwdriver held in your hand. If the insulation on the handle is thin or cracked, the current could jump to you. Furthermore, simply shorting the terminals (touching both at once) creates a dead short that is hard on the equipment and potentially your eyes if it arcs.

2. The Resistor Method (The "Pro" Way)

The safest way to dissipate the charge is to bleed it off slowly using a high-wattage resistor (usually 20k to 100k ohms, rated for 5-10 watts).

  • Attach one end of the resistor to a grounded wire (the microwave chassis).
  • Attach the other end to a well-insulated probe.
  • Touch the probe to the capacitor terminal for about 10–15 seconds.
  • This converts the stored energy into a tiny bit of heat rather than a violent spark.

3. The "Two-Screwdriver" or "Insulated Jumper" Method

If you don't have a resistor setup, you use the chassis as the "sink":

  1. Ground the Tool: Take a clip lead (alligator clip) and connect the metal shaft of a highly insulated screwdriver to the metal frame (chassis) of the microwave.
  2. Touch the Terminal: While keeping one hand in your pocket (to prevent a path through your heart if something goes wrong), touch the screwdriver tip to each terminal of the capacitor.
  3. Cross the Terminals: Finally, short the two terminals of the capacitor together with the screwdriver to ensure no potential difference remains between them.

Critical Safety Rules:

  • The "One Hand" Rule: Always keep one hand behind your back or in your pocket when working near high-voltage components. This ensures that if you do take a shock, the path isn't "hand-to-hand" across your chest.
  • Unplug First: It sounds obvious, but always double-check that the unit has been unplugged for at least a few minutes. Most modern microwaves have "bleeder resistors" built-in that should drain the charge automatically, but you should never trust them to work.
  • Verify with a Meter: If you have a multimeter rated for high voltage, check the terminals after discharging to ensure the reading is at 0V.

Given your interest in KiCad and PCB design, building a simple "discharge stick" with a few high-voltage resistors in series is a great afternoon project that will make your workbench a lot safer.

turns.prompt_text: So this microwave has been unplugged for probably weeks now. however, I would still like to be able to use a multimeter or some way to see if the capacitor has wattage
turns.response_html:
It’s a smart move to verify with a meter even after weeks of sitting. While most microwave capacitors have an internal "bleeder resistor" designed to drain the charge over time, those resistors can and do fail. If it fails, the capacitor can hold that charge indefinitely.

Since you have a Fluke 8842A and a Milwaukee digital multimeter, you have the right tools, but you need to be very careful with the execution.

How to Safely Check for Stored Energy

First, a quick technical correction: you aren't looking for wattage (which is a measure of power over time, $P = VI$); you are looking for Voltage ($V$), which represents the electrical potential currently "waiting" in the capacitor.

1. Set the Meter Correctly

  • Mode: Set your multimeter to DC Voltage (V⎓).
  • Range: If your meter isn't auto-ranging, set it to the highest possible voltage scale (usually 600V or 1000V).
  • Important Limitation: A standard handheld multimeter is usually rated for 600V to 1000V CAT III. A fully charged microwave capacitor can be 2,000V+.
    • If the microwave was recently plugged in: Do NOT use your multimeter first; you will blow the internal fuse or destroy the meter.
    • Since it's been weeks: It is likely safe to check with the meter, as any remaining "ghost" charge should be well within the meter's 600V–1000V range.

2. The Measurement Process

  1. Chassis Ground: Clip your black (negative) lead to the metal chassis of the microwave using one of your alligator clips. This keeps one hand free (The "One Hand Rule").
  2. Probe: With your other hand, touch the red (positive) probe to one of the capacitor terminals.
  3. Check Both: Check both terminals. Then, check the voltage across the two terminals (red on one, black on the other).
  4. The Goal: You are looking for a reading as close to 0V as possible. Anything over 30V is generally considered the threshold where it can start to be "felt," but with a microwave cap, you want it dead-flat before touching it.

If You See Voltage

If the meter shows a reading (e.g., 50V or 100V), you still need to discharge it using the resistor method mentioned earlier. Since you have a supply of resistors in your kit, you can actually make a temporary bleed-down tool:

  1. Take a high-value resistor (something like 100kΩ).
  2. Use your alligator clips to connect one side of the resistor to the chassis and the other side to a screwdriver tip.
  3. Hold the screwdriver by the insulated handle and touch the terminal.
  4. Watch the voltage drop on your Fluke in real-time. It’s actually pretty satisfying to watch the potential energy drain away safely.

Pro-Tip for your Fluke 8842A

Since that's a high-precision bench meter, it’s excellent for this, but just remember that bench tops often have lower transient protection than rugged handhelds like your Milwaukee. For the initial "is this thing live" tap, the Milwaukee handheld is generally the "tougher" choice for field work.

turns.prompt_text: I have mainly pretty small ones. would a light bulb work instead?
turns.response_html:
That is a classic "hacker" trick, and yes, an incandescent light bulb works brilliantly for this. In fact, it's often preferred because it gives you a visual confirmation: if the bulb flashes and then goes dark, you know the energy is gone.

However, there are a few important "gotchas" to make this safe:

1. The Type of Bulb Matters

  • Must be Incandescent: Use an old-school filament bulb (like a 40W or 60W bulb). The tungsten filament acts as a high-voltage resistor.
  • Do NOT use LED or CFL: These have complex circuitry (drivers and ballasts) inside them that can blow up or fail instantly when hit with a high-voltage DC spike from a capacitor. They won't bleed the charge reliably.

2. How to Set It Up

Since you have a 28-piece electrical clip set, this is easy to rig up safely:

  1. The Socket: Ideally, use a standard light socket with two wires coming out.
  2. The Connection: * Clip one wire to the microwave chassis (ground).
    • Clip the other wire to the shaft of a well-insulated screwdriver.
  3. The Discharge: Hold the screwdriver by the handle and touch the tip to the capacitor terminals.
  4. The Result: You might see a brief, dim glow from the filament. Once the glow is gone (or if there is no glow after a few seconds), the capacitor is discharged.

Why small resistors are risky

The reason your small 1/4 watt resistors aren't ideal is voltage breakdown. Standard small resistors are usually only rated for about 200V to 250V. If you put 2,000V across one, the electricity might just jump over the resistor (arcing), or the resistor could pop like a firecracker.

A light bulb is designed to handle "mains" voltage, and while a microwave cap is higher than that, the vacuum/gas inside the bulb is much better at handling a brief high-voltage pulse than a tiny piece of carbon film.

Final Verification

Even after the light bulb trick, always follow up with your Milwaukee multimeter.

  1. Discharge with the bulb.
  2. Measure with the meter.
  3. If it reads 0.00V, you are clear to start harvesting those microswitches and that transformer.
